Chapter 02

Key Findings

The evidence points first to restoring delivery, improving comparable local cost data and protecting households with household-based support.

Bottom line

Luxembourg should put the first policy emphasis on restoring a dependable housing-supply pipeline and converting permits into completed homes. Local targeting should combine observed housing costs with demand and feasibility evidence. The available commune rent data cover only 36 of 100 communes, so the project no longer recommends using a national commune index as an allocation rule. Income support should remain household-based.

01

Permits weakened while population grew

Authorized dwellings fell from 6,079 in 2021 to 3,538 in 2025 (−41.8%), while population rose from 634,730 to 681,973 (+7.4%).

The near-term supply pipeline moved in the wrong direction. Permits are not completions, so completion tracking is the next essential measurement.

02

Household formation and occupied stock were close over the last census decade

From 2011 to 2021, private households increased by 41,760 and inhabited dwellings by 42,365.

The decade totals broadly matched, but they do not show location, suitability, tenure, vacancy, or affordability. The post-2021 permit fall remains a warning signal.

03

Market housing costs outpaced average gross earnings

From 2013 to 2025, average annual gross earnings rose 45.7%, advertised monthly rent rose 50.0%, and existing-apartment prices per m² rose 86.9%.

Monthly advertised rent is the main rent comparison. Advertised rents are asking prices, not signed contracts.

04

The raw rent-per-m² history is composition-sensitive

Monthly rent divided by rent per m² gives an implied size proxy that falls from 68.7 m² in 2013 to 45.4 m² in 2025.

This ratio uses two averages and is not a measured mean size, but its movement shows that the raw per-m² series should not support a long-run headline. The official methodology also warns that surface and market composition affect advertised-rent statistics.

05

Overall purchasing power improved, but that does not resolve housing access

CPI-adjusted average gross-earnings purchasing power was 14.9% above its 2013 index level in 2025.

General purchasing power and access to market housing can diverge; CP04 is not used as a market-housing-price measure.

06

No clear poverty-housing-cost link was found

The income-poverty rate was 14.9% in 2009 and 14.8% in 2025. The change regression has 16 observations, R²=0.07, and p=0.62 for monthly rent growth.

The model has little explanatory power and no statistically clear rent relationship. Household-level linked rent, income, and tenure data are needed.

07

Commune rent evidence is selected toward larger places

Rents are published for 36 communes with mean 2025 population 13,762, versus 64 suppressed communes averaging 2,915.

The 36-commune rent regression must not be generalized to all 100 communes.

Policy priorities

01

Restore and stabilize the delivery pipeline. Set a measurable path back above the 2021 permit level, but manage it with separate indicators for permits, starts, completions, delivery time, tenure, and location. A mechanical 20% increase over 2025 would still leave permits below 2021.

02

Do not allocate nationally from incomplete commune rankings. The replacement score includes monthly advertised rent relative to P10 individual salary, population growth, and one-person-household share. It drops dwelling density, which cancelled the household-size component. Because rents are published for only 36 communes, scenario B is now a selected-sample illustration, not a national allocation rule. Extend comparable cost evidence before using it for funding decisions.

03

Protect lower-income households with household-based measures. Calibrate allowances and social-rental access using actual household disposable income, rent paid, household size, and tenure. Do not turn a single-earner salary-to-average-advertised-rent ratio into a subsidy estimate.

04

Monitor affordability with market-specific series. Track advertised and contracted rents, transaction prices, wages, disposable income, poverty, and completions. Use annual CPI averages for general purchasing power and label CP04 as housing, water, and energy consumption prices—not as market rent or purchase prices.

05

Treat commune regression results as exploratory. Publication thresholds remove smaller markets. Decisions need local feasibility evidence and comparable housing costs, not the selected rent regression or score alone.

Chapter 10

Statistical Analysis

Relationships are descriptive and selected-sample estimates, not causal evidence.

The rent regression is exploratory and limited to communes meeting the publication threshold. It is not causal and is not representative of all 100 communes.

12

Chapter 12

Data Library & Methodology

Every table remains available here with chapter filters, search and CSV export.

Observed data and scenarios are separated. Missing or suppressed values remain missing. Every analytical commune join uses the audited canonical current-commune code read as text. Observatoire and salary labels are used only to build the crosswalk where source codes do not align with current official commune codes. The raw rent-per-m² history is composition-sensitive; monthly advertised rent is the primary historical rent measure.
